title: The First Daughter
full_review:
In the fluffy and formulaic romantic comedy "The First Daughter" (20th Century Fox), Katie Holmes plays Samantha Mackenzie, a college freshman trying to fit in on campus; the only problem is, her father happens to be the leader of the free world.

Michael Keaton plays her commander-in-chief dad whose eyebrows arch in paternal perturbation whenever Samantha implores him to pare down the phalanx of Secret Service agents shadowing her every move so she have a little fun.

Her efforts to enjoy a "normal" college experience are aided by her sassy dorm roommate (played by pop singer Amerie) and hampered by her two men-in-black handlers (Michael Milhoan and Dwayne Adway).

Further complications arise when Samantha falls for cute resident adviser James (Marc Blucas), prompting a visit from first mom Margaret Colin when the fallout from the knotty romance threatens her dad's bid for re-election.

Of course being the president's daughter has its advantages: Air Force One is a great way to impress your friends.

Laced with fairy-tale elements, "The First Daughter" was originally slated to open earlier in the year, but 20th Century Fox decided to push back its release date to give the movie some separation from the similarly themed -- and equally forgettable -- "Chasing Liberty."

Holmes is appealing enough, but the film proves a disappointing follow-up to last year's "Pieces of April."

Though targeting the 'tweener crowd, this lightweight fantasy, directed by Forest Whitaker, contains some behavior inappropriate for -- and unwelcome in -- a PG-rated movie, including a lewd rendition of "Hail to the Chief" by a quartet of fraternity pledges, a joke about birth control and a scene where a miniskirted Samantha dances drunkenly atop a bar.

At one point, James tells Samantha, "Sometimes you have to break the rules; you never know when you're going to get something inspired." No chance of that here.

Due to underaged drinking and implied sexual situations, as well as some crude language and humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
